title: Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis (PrEP)
body:

It is a design, not an established fact and not a tested public-health recommendation: its effectiveness is unknown until it is properly evaluated, and it must never be read as a replacement for established prevention or clinical care. HIV is the virus and AIDS is the syndrome that can follow untreated infection, so prevention means stopping HIV transmission. There is no general cure for HIV, and nothing in this design claims one. See a clinician or an HIV testing service for advice about your own situation.

The Signature PrEP Companion is an original Signature design: a personal prevention planner that pairs a PrEP schedule with adherence support and testing reminders in one plain-language dashboard. It is a design, not an established product, and its effectiveness is unknown until evaluated. The companion tracks daily pill-taking or injection appointments, records doses taken, and flags gaps early so the user can contact a clinician before protection lapses.

The design works in three parts. A schedule keeper holds the dosing plan agreed with a clinician, with reminders timed to the user's day. An adherence journal lets the user log each dose or appointment with one tap and note side effects or problems. A testing calendar books the next HIV test, kidney check, and sexual-health screen, and sends reminders ahead of each one. Nothing in the design dispenses medicine or changes a dose; every medical decision stays with the clinician.

Because this is an unevaluated design, no effectiveness figure can be stated for it. Its intended benefit is indirect: by making missed doses visible sooner and testing dates harder to forget, it aims to support the adherence on which real PrEP depends. That benefit is hypothetical until tested in a proper study. The design does not protect against other sexually transmitted infections or pregnancy, and it does not replace condoms or clinician follow-up.

Access to the design would be through a clinic-linked program: a clinician sets the plan, the user carries the planner, and the clinic reviews adherence and testing at visits. Limits include dependence on the user keeping the log honestly, phone access, and privacy of health data stored on a device. Anyone interested should see a clinician or an HIV testing service to discuss real PrEP options first, and treat this design as a support idea, not as prevention itself.

title: Post-Exposure Prophylaxis (PEP)
body:

See a clinician or an HIV testing service for advice about your own situation.

The Signature 72-Hour Rapid-Response Card is an original Signature design: a wallet-sized action card and phone companion that walks a person through the first hours after a possible HIV exposure. It is a design, not an established service, and its effectiveness is unknown until evaluated. The card lists, in order, the steps to take: seek emergency care at once, note the time of exposure, and bring a list of current medicines.

The design works by removing delay and guesswork. One side of the card gives the nearest 24-hour services and a script for what to say on arrival. The phone companion records the exposure time, starts a countdown to the 72-hour limit, and holds the 28-day course calendar with daily reminders. A check-in prompt each week asks about side effects and offers a one-tap message to the treating service. The design never decides whether PEP is appropriate; only a clinician does that.

Because this is an unevaluated design, no effectiveness figure can be stated. Its intended benefit is faster arrival at care and better completion of the 28-day course, both of which are known to matter for real PEP. That benefit is hypothetical until tested. The design cannot extend the 72-hour window, cannot prescribe, and cannot confirm whether infection occurred; only follow-up testing can do that.

Access to the design would be through clinics and emergency services that hand out the card at testing visits and community events. Limits include phone access, language availability, and the risk that a person treats the card as a substitute for going to care. Anyone with a possible exposure should go to an emergency service immediately and see a clinician or an HIV testing service for follow-up, whether or not they carry the card.

It is a design, not an established product, and its effectiveness is unknown until evaluated. The kit holds a sizing guide, a small stock of latex and non-latex options, water-based lubricant sachets, and a plain-language illustrated instruction card.

The design works by tackling the two commonest failure causes: wrong fit and damage before use. The sizing guide matches width to comfort without tightness or looseness. A pre-use check panel reminds the user to check the expiry date, feel for air in the wrapper, and look for tears. The instruction card shows the steps for putting on, lubricating, and removing a condom, and a QR-style code links to a clinic demonstration video. The kit contains no medicine and makes no medical claim.

The kit does not make a condom fully effective, and it does not replace testing or other prevention methods.

Access to the design would be through clinics, community organizations, and free-distribution programs, alongside existing condom supplies. Limits include the need for honest sizing, storage away from heat, and user willingness to follow the card. Anyone wanting a demonstration should see a clinician or an HIV testing service, and treat this kit as a support idea, not as prevention itself.

The Signature Test-Reminder Circle is an original Signature design: a private reminder system that schedules a person's HIV tests, tracks window periods, and links results to next steps. It is a design, not an established service, and its effectiveness is unknown until evaluated. The user enters their last test date and risk pattern, and the circle proposes the next test date, explains why a repeat test may be needed after a recent exposure, and stores clinic contact details.

The design works in three parts. A calendar holds test dates and sends reminders a week and a day ahead. A window-period explainer shows, in plain language, why a test taken too soon after an exposure may need repeating, without interpreting any result. A linkage panel lists what to do after each kind of result: a negative result with ongoing risk leads to prevention options, and a positive screening result leads to confirmatory testing and a clinic appointment. The design never reads a test result and never gives a diagnosis.

Because this is an unevaluated design, no effectiveness figure can be stated. Its intended benefit is indirect: fewer missed tests and faster linkage to confirmatory testing and care. That benefit is hypothetical until tested. The design cannot detect HIV, cannot shorten the window period, and cannot replace laboratory confirmation of any screening result.

Access to the design would be through testing services that offer it at the point of testing, with data held on the user's own device. Limits include phone access, privacy, and the risk that reminders create a false sense of safety after a test taken inside the window period. Anyone unsure about testing should see a clinician or an HIV testing service for advice on which test to take and when to repeat it.

title: Needle and Syringe Safety and Harm-Reduction Services
body:
Signature edition note and language frame. This record is an original Signature prevention design, labeled signature-original throughout. It is a design, not an established fact and not a tested public-health recommendation: its effectiveness is unknown until it is properly evaluated, and it must never be read as a replacement for established prevention or clinical care. HIV is the virus and AIDS is the syndrome that can follow untreated infection, so prevention means stopping HIV transmission. There is no general cure for HIV, and nothing in this design claims one. See a clinician or an HIV testing service for advice about your own situation.

The Signature Safe-Kit Exchange Post is an original Signature design: a community harm-reduction point that combines sterile-equipment distribution with testing linkage and a discreet digital check-in. It is a design, not an established service, and its effectiveness is unknown until evaluated. The post stocks sterile needles and syringes, ancillary sterile items, sharps containers, and information cards, and offers on-site or referred HIV and hepatitis testing.

The design works by lowering every barrier to a safe injection at once. A no-questions counter gives out enough sterile equipment for every injection, not a ration that forces reuse. A returns bin accepts used sharps without recording who returned them. A check-in screen, usable without giving a name, lets a person book a test, request a wound-care slot, or ask for a referral to drug treatment or HIV care. Staff are trained in non-judgmental engagement, and no one is required to commit to abstinence to use the post.

Because this is an unevaluated design, no effectiveness figure can be stated. Its intended benefit is indirect: fuller coverage of sterile equipment and faster linkage to testing and care, both of which are associated with fewer infections in real syringe programs. That benefit is hypothetical until tested. The design does not itself treat drug dependence, does not test for HIV on the spot unless a testing service is attached, and does not remove sexual-transmission risk.

Access to the design would be through public-health departments and community organizations, placed where people who inject drugs already gather. Limits include local law, funding, safe staffing, and the need for genuine confidentiality. Anyone who injects drugs should see a clinician or an HIV testing service for testing and for links to local harm-reduction services, and treat this design as a service idea, not as a substitute for sterile equipment and testing.

title: Education and Stigma Reduction
body:
Signature edition note and language frame. This record is an original Signature prevention design, labeled signature-original throughout. It is a design, not an established fact and not a tested public-health recommendation: its effectiveness is unknown until it is properly evaluated, and it must never be read as a replacement for established prevention or clinical care. HIV is the virus and AIDS is the syndrome that can follow untreated infection, so prevention means stopping HIV transmission. There is no general cure for HIV, and nothing in this design claims one. See a clinician or an HIV testing service for advice about your own situation.

The Signature Stigma-Free Classroom is an original Signature design: a school and workplace education program built around accurate information, contact with people living with HIV, and service links. It is a design, not an established curriculum, and its effectiveness is unknown until evaluated. Each module pairs a short fact session with a discussion led by a trained facilitator, including, where willing, a speaker living with HIV.

The design works in three modules. Module one covers transmission facts and myths, treatment, and U=U in plain language. Module two explores stigma: how language, jokes, and policies exclude people, and what respectful language looks like. Module three connects learning to services: where to test, how partner services work, and how to support a friend who discloses a diagnosis. Every module ends with a local service list, so information leads directly to a clinic door.

The Signature Lube-Match Card is an original Signature design: a pocket compatibility card that matches condom material to safe lubricant types at a glance. It is a design, not an established product, and its effectiveness is unknown until evaluated. One side lists latex, polyurethane, and polyisoprene condoms against water-based, silicone-based, and oil-based lubricants with safe-or-unsafe marks. The other side lists common household oils to avoid with latex.

The design works by removing the commonest error: reaching for an oil-based product with a latex condom. The card uses color and symbols rather than text alone, so it works across literacy levels, and a small sachet holder keeps a compatible lubricant with the condoms. A clinic version adds a space for the user's preferred products, filled in with staff at a condom demonstration. The card contains no medicine and makes no claim that lubricant prevents HIV.

Because this is an unevaluated design, no effectiveness figure can be stated. Its intended benefit is indirect: fewer compatibility mistakes should mean fewer condom breaks, which is how lubricant choice affects real protection. That benefit is hypothetical until tested. The card cannot detect a damaged condom, cannot replace condoms, and cannot help if no compatible lubricant is available.

Access to the design would be through clinics and condom-distribution programs, tucked into condom packs. Limits include keeping the card legible, covering all local product types, and language availability. Anyone unsure about a product should check its label or see a clinician or an HIV testing service for advice on condom and lubricant combinations.
